1. J. L. Nancy, The Birth to Presence (US: Stanford University Press, 1993), 320.

4. Nancy, Corpus (US: Fordham University Press, 2008).
5. M. Bakhtin, Rabelais and his World (Indiana University Press, 1984).
6. G. Bataille, Death and Sensuality: A Study of Eroticism and the Taboo (Walker and Company,
1962), 44.
7. "… not subject to a treatise." (51)
8. Nancy's emphasis (33).
9. Exposition" doesn't mean that intimacy is extracted from its withdrawal, and carried
outside, put on display. Because then the body would be an exposition of the "self," in the
sense of a translation, an interpretation, or a staging. "Exposition," on the contrary, means
that expression itself is an intimacy and a withdrawal. The a-part-self is not translated or
incarnated into exposition, it is what it is there: this vertiginous withdrawal of the self from
the self that is needed to open the infinity of that withdrawal all the way up to self. The body
is this departure of self to self. (Corpus, 33)
10. Corpus, 86.
12. Derrida, Points, 163.
13. Derrida evokes a delicate episode in Nancy's own life course which is his heart
transplant which he relates in his book L'Intrus and which would deeply impact his
conception of himself and the other. (257)
